title: Wireless Electricity: When Can We Unplug Our TVs?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore wireless electricity, or wireless power transfer. They trace history from Nikola Tesla's experiments and Heinrich Hertz's 1880s radio work, through William Brown of Raytheon's 1964 helicopter demonstration and the 1975 NASA JPL microwave power record, and the 2024 Korean Space Agency record. They explain near-field charging (electric toothbrushes, induction, Qi standard, MagSafe) and far-field approaches (microwaves, lasers, RFID tags, resonant induction). They discuss inefficiency (around 20 percent end-to-end), safety concerns, wireless EV charging lanes, Ossia's Cota system and Forever batteries, Energous/Motorola-Guru charger ideas, DARPA's PERSISTENT OWER concept, New Zealand's EMROD towers, and Caltech's 2023 space solar power demonstration. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from Mark Konts about Sources of Strength.

segments.title: Tour dates announcement
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh announce upcoming live tour dates in several US cities and direct listeners to the website or link for tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Tech Stuff Edition framing and joke about how wires and plugs are a nuisance, setting up a discussion of wireless electricity.

segments.title: History: Tesla, Hertz, and early wireless power
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh describe Heinrich Hertz's 1880s radio energy transmission and Tesla's wireless experiments, including the unverified legend of lighting bulbs about 25 miles from his Colorado station.

segments.title: Records: Raytheon helicopter and JPL 1975 transmission
segments.summary: William Brown of Raytheon kept a helicopter aloft for ten hours in 1964 using microwave power. NASA JPL's 1975 long-distance transmission record, about 1.5 to 4 kilometers, was broken in 2024 by the Korean Space Agency by a small margin.
topics: Korean Space Agency wireless power record

segments.title: Near-field charging: toothbrushes, induction, and Qi
segments.summary: The hosts explain near-field wireless charging, including electric toothbrushes using inductive coupling, resonant induction, and Nokia's early wireless charger followed by the Qi standard from the Wireless Power Consortium.

segments.title: MagSafe and magnetic alignment
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Apple's MagSafe chargers, which use magnets to align coils for more efficient charging of around 15 to 20 watts, and Chuck mentions a car charger he uses.

segments.title: Qi2 and cross-brand compatibility
segments.summary: Josh explains that the Qi2 protocol lets Android and iPhone share the same charger, reducing packaging and manufacturing costs.

segments.title: Wireless charging for electric cars and roads
segments.summary: The hosts discuss garage pad charging for EVs and the idea of embedding wireless charging coils in an expressway lane so cars charge while driving.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Chuck announces a break before returning to the show.

segments.title: Roadside etiquette tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about driving long distances and then discuss not leaving urine bottles or dental floss on the roadside.

segments.title: Far-field wireless transfer methods
segments.summary: The hosts explain far-field transfer using microwaves, lasers, and millimeter waves, requiring a conversion from electricity to electromagnetic energy and back, and note consumer products exist but are costly and slow.

segments.title: RFID tags and Internet of Things
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh describe RFID tags that get power from radio waves and reply with an ID, used in warehouse inventory, and suggest wireless power could help Internet of Things sensors.

segments.title: Replacing batteries and the Ossia Cota system
segments.summary: The hosts discuss replacing disposable batteries and pacemaker surgeries, then describe Ossia's Cota system, a room transmitter, and Forever batteries that contain receivers.

segments.title: Motorola and Guru wireless charger
segments.summary: Guru and Motorola debuted an over-the-air charger that can charge multiple phones up to ten feet away, but it has not reached market. Josh mentions Arlo wireless power security cameras.

segments.title: Security cameras and public spaces
segments.summary: Chuck comments on the limited crime-fighting value of home security cameras, and the hosts suggest wireless charging could be used in public transit and airports.

segments.title: Efficiency problems and cost tradeoffs
segments.summary: Josh says wireless power transfer through beams is roughly 20 percent efficient, contrasts this with the JPL's 49 percent over a mile, and argues the wasted energy is cheap compared to disposable batteries.
topics: cost of batteries versus wasted electricity

segments.title: Safety of room-based and beam charging
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Ossia system bouncing signals around a room and only delivering power when needed. They discuss safety concerns such as heating conductive objects, microwave and laser hazards, and automatic shutoff when obstructed.

segments.title: DARPA PERSISTENT OWER military applications
segments.summary: Chuck describes DARPA's proposed PERSISTENT OWER concept of beaming power from aircraft to disaster or conflict zones. Josh notes military applications and that inefficiency is still more efficient than hauling fuel.

segments.title: Military to consumer tech trickle-down
segments.summary: Josh notes military R&D often trickles down into consumer products, and that wireless power could follow the same path.

segments.title: EMROD New Zealand power towers
segments.summary: Josh describes EMROD's line-of-sight towers in New Zealand that beam energy between towers, comparing this to Lord of the Rings beacon fires and Wi-Fi, and suggesting wind energy could be moved to urban areas.

segments.title: Space solar power and Caltech
segments.summary: Chuck describes space-based solar satellites beaming microwaves to Earth, and says Caltech's Space Power Project sent a detectable amount of energy from a satellite to Earth in 2023. Josh calls space solar a step toward a Dyson sphere.

segments.title: Listener mail from Mark Konts on Sources of Strength
segments.summary: Mark Konts, an art therapist in Springfield, Ohio, describes the Sources of Strength wellness and suicide prevention program in schools and points listeners to its websites.

segments.title: Listener mail call to action
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send stories about their own community work to the show's email address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the show's production credit and promotional information.
